He stood up and left the room with my nurse, and a moment later my father came in.

Nothing could have brought me greater happiness at that instant than the arrival of my father. I reached out my hand and cried,

“Then you are safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father reassured me that they were well, and tried to lift my despair by talking about the people so dear to my heart. But he soon realised that a prison was no place for cheerfulness. “What a place you are living in, my son!” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the room’s miserable condition. “You set out in search of happiness, but some fatal misfortune seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—”

Hearing the name of my unfortunate, murdered friend upset me more than my weakened condition could bear. I began to weep.

“Oh, yes, Father,” I replied. “Some destiny of the most terrible kind hangs over me, and I must stay alive to fulfil it. Otherwise, surely I would have died upon Henry’s coffin.”

We were not allowed to talk for long. My health was so fragile that every possible precaution had to be taken to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that I must not exhaust myself through too much effort. But my father’s appearance had been like the coming of my guardian angel, and gradually my health returned.

As the illness left me, I sank into a dark, oppressive melancholy that nothing could dispel. Clerval’s image was constantly before my eyes, ghastly and murdered. More than once these thoughts distressed me so deeply that my friends feared a dangerous relapse. Oh, why did they preserve a life so miserable and so hated? Surely it was so that I could fulfil the destiny now approaching its end. Soon—very soon—death will still this pounding heart and release me from the enormous burden of anguish that crushes me into the dust. In carrying out the sentence of justice, I too will find rest. At that time, death still seemed far away, though the desire for it never left my thoughts. I often sat for hours without moving or speaking, longing for some tremendous upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The time for the court’s sessions drew near. I had already spent three months in prison, and though I remained weak and constantly at risk of a relapse, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court was sitting. Mr. Kirwin took responsibility for all the work of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence.

They had sent these representatives to Adrian, who had been chosen to settle the dispute. The men had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and a deserted countryside, nursing their fierce hatred of one another all the way. Now each argued his side with undiminished loyalty to his own faction.

By questioning the representatives separately and investigating at length, we discovered the true situation in Paris. Ever since parliament chose him as Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had accepted Adrian’s authority. He was the captain who would lead us from our homeland into unfamiliar countries, the maker of our laws, and our protector. When we first planned our departure, we had not expected any part of our company to remain separated from the rest. Authority over the whole group rose through successive ranks to the Earl of Windsor. But unexpected events altered our plans, and most of our people were separated from their supreme leader for nearly two months. They had crossed over in two separate groups, and disagreement broke out between them after they reached Paris.

They had found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, returning travellers and merchants, together with letters, regularly brought us news of the disease’s destruction on the continent. But as deaths increased, these exchanges grew fewer and finally stopped. Even within England, news passed slowly and rarely from one part of the island to another. No ship crossed the waters between Calais and Dover. If some sorrowful traveller left the French coast to return among us, hoping to discover whether his relatives were alive or dead, the greedy sea often swallowed his little boat. Or he caught the disease after a day or two and died before he could describe the ruin of France. We therefore knew very little about conditions on the continent, and still vaguely hoped to find many companions somewhere in that vast territory. But the same forces that had so terribly reduced England’s population had caused even greater destruction in its neighbouring country. France was empty. Along the entire road from Calais to Paris, not a single human being had been found. In Paris a few remained, perhaps a hundred. Accepting their approaching fate, they drifted through the capital’s streets and gathered to talk about the past, with the liveliness and even cheerfulness that so rarely desert the people of that nation.

The English occupied Paris without opposition. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at the usual meeting place in the Tuileries. They wondered why these islanders would come to their doomed city. For people suffering extreme misery always imagine their own share of a disaster to be the bitterest. In the same way, when we endure intense pain, we would gladly exchange the particular agony tormenting us for any other that attacked a different part of the body.

“I agree. That’s the best way. Shall we just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh, no, that won’t do for this. That’s fine for ordinary little things that don’t matter—especially with girls, because they’ll break their word anyway and tell everything if they get angry. But something this big ought to be written down. And there ought to be blood.”

Tom approved of the idea with his whole heart. It was mysterious, dark, and dreadful; the time of night, their situation, and their surroundings all suited it. He picked up a clean pine roof shingle lying in the moonlight and took a small piece of red marking chalk from his pocket. Positioning the wood where the moon lit it, he slowly and painfully scratched out the following words. With every downward stroke he gripped his tongue between his teeth, easing the pressure as his hand moved upward.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear They will keep quiet about This and They hope They will Fall down dead where They stand if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry marvelled at Tom’s skill with writing and the grandeur of his words. He immediately pulled a pin from his jacket lapel and was about to prick himself, but Tom interrupted.

“Wait! Don’t use that. Pins are brass. There might be green rust on it.”

“What’s green rust?”

“Poison, that’s what. Just try swallowing some once—you’ll find out.”

So Tom removed the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the fleshy part of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After a while, and a great deal of squeezing, Tom managed to write his initials, using the tip of his little finger as a pen. Then he taught Huckleberry to form an H and an F, and their oath was finished. They buried the shingle near the wall with gloomy rituals and muttered spells, believing that their tongues were now chained shut and the key thrown away.

Someone slipped quietly through a gap at the far end of the ruined building, but neither boy noticed.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this mean we can never tell—ever?”

“Of course. Whatever happens, we’ve got to keep quiet. We’d fall down dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yes, I guess that’s true.”

They kept whispering for a little while. Then a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside, less than ten feet away. The boys suddenly clutched each other in terror.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—look through the crack. Hurry!”

“No, you look, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”
